title: Nankana Sahib, 1921
hook: reformers seeking to free gurdwaras from corrupt keepers are killed at Guru Nanak's birthplace

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jallianwala Bagh, and the Vaisakhi it changed. Did you pause to remember someone in the middle of something good? Today, two years later, a different kind of struggle, and a vow not to strike back. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

A family keeps one precious place: the house where a great-great-grandmother was born. The caretaker hired to look after it starts treating it as his own. He charges people to come in. He does as he likes inside. When the family complains, the authorities side with him. What would you do in their place? In the early 1920s, many Sikhs faced that question about their historic gurdwaras, including the one at the place where Guru Nanak was born. Today: the Akali.
screen: `A FAMILY'S PRECIOUS PLACE.` → `A CARETAKER WHO ACTS LIKE THE OWNER.` → `GURU NANAK'S BIRTHPLACE.`

segments.voice: Akali means one who belongs to Akal, the Timeless: the old name for God we met at the Akal Takht. In the 1920s it became the name of a movement. By then many historic gurdwaras were run by mahants, hereditary custodians who had come to treat the shrines and their lands as private property. Some did it well. Others let practices creep in that went against the Gurus' teaching, and some were accused of corruption and worse. The colonial government mostly backed them. So Sikhs formed jathas, bands of volunteers, to take the gurdwaras back into community care. And they made a vow: they would not use violence, even if attacked. On the twentieth of February, 1921, a jatha led by Bhai Lachhman Singh went at dawn to Gurdwara Janam Asthan at Nankana Sahib, the place of Guru Nanak's birth, to pray and ask for its handover. The mahant there had prepared for them. His hired men shut the gates and attacked the Sikhs with guns, swords and axes. The jatha did not fight back. The counts differ: official figures were lower, and Sikh accounts say well over a hundred were killed. Bhai Lachhman Singh was tied to a tree and burned. The tree still stands at the gurdwara. The news shook all of India. Leaders from across the country came to Nankana Sahib, and the government was forced to act against the mahant. The vow held. Peaceful, and firm. Within days, the shrine passed into the care of a Sikh committee. Tomorrow, where the movement went next.
screen: `AKALI — ONE WHO BELONGS TO THE TIMELESS.` · `MAHANTS TREAT SHRINES AS PROPERTY.` · `JATHAS VOW NOT TO STRIKE BACK.` · `NANKANA SAHIB, 20 FEBRUARY 1921.` · then, large: `PEACEFUL, AND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Think of the last time someone provoked you: a sharp comment, a rude driver, an unfair email. Recall the moment. Now picture yourself in that moment again, but this time you keep your feet planted and your voice calm. You don't give up what's right. You just don't strike back. Breathe into that feeling of being both steady and unbending. Decide to try it once today, if the moment comes. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Akali. One who belongs to the Timeless, and the name of the 1920s movement whose volunteers vowed to free the gurdwaras without violence.
Your line: peaceful, and firm. Today, stay peaceful once when provoked, without giving up what's right. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the martyrs of Nankana Sahib each February, and the jand tree where Bhai Lachhman Singh was killed is preserved at Gurdwara Janam Asthan; pilgrims from India travel there for Guru Nanak's birth anniversary.

fork.reveal: the jatha did not fight back. many were killed, and the news shook all of India.

original.note: Gurmukhi: akali, one who belongs to Akal, the Timeless.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh political party.
what it means: one who belongs to the Timeless, and the 1920s movement that freed gurdwaras through nonviolent struggle.

what a scholar hears: the gurdwara reform (Akali) movement of 1920–25; the Nankana Sahib killings of 20 February 1921 under Mahant Narain Das; casualty figures range from about 86 (official) to 130–150 or more (Sikh sources). The party Shiromani Akali Dal grew from the movement.

sources.ref: The Nankana Sahib massacre, 20 February 1921, and the Akali movement, as recorded in Sikh history

notes: Casualty numbers vary (official figures lower; Sikh sources around 130–150+); script says 'more than a hundred ... many sources say around 130 or more'. Confirm.
Bhai Lachhman Singh (Dharowali) tied to the jand tree and burned: confirm as recorded.
Mahants described as mixed (some good, some corrupt) to avoid blanket blame; confirm.
Nankana Sahib is now in Pakistan; not mentioned here because Partition is two days away.

Review (fresh editor): hook no longer opens 'Imagine' and drops the superlative 'holiest'; the casualty line said 'more than a hundred' as fact, but the official count was about 86, so it now says the counts differ; replaced the stock ending with what followed (the shrine handed to a Sikh committee); the practice no longer tells the listener what they felt.
